name: Absolutism (European history)
summary: Absolutism holds that sovereign power should rest wholly in a monarch, unrestrained by legislatures, churches or social elites. It is justified by divine right and by the theory that sovereignty is indivisible and perpetual, though classic theorists still bind the ruler to natural and divine law. In practice it centralised law, built standing armies and bureaucracies, subordinated the church and favoured mercantilist economics.
scope: Classical European absolutism of roughly 1600 to 1789: monarchical power that is not subject to regularized challenge by church, legislature, nobility or courts, justified by divine right of kings and by indivisible sovereignty (Britannica, s5, s6, s8). Its defining sources name Louis XIV as the epitome, Bossuet and James I as its theorists and, with the dispute noted by the Stanford Encyclopedia, Bodin (s2). Britannica notes the same label is also used for modern dictators (s5) and for Hobbes's pragmatic case; this audit covers the early modern European doctrine only, and excludes enlightened absolutism and modern dictatorships.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Britannica records appeal to God as sanctioning hereditary right, and hereditary kingship is the rank absolutism rests on.

clerical-rule.rationale: Bossuet makes the king God's lieutenant who holds supreme power, and Britannica notes the new monarchs tended to become heads of the church as well as the state.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Bossuet says the prince need render account of his acts to no one, and Britannica says divine right made kings answerable to no earthly authority such as a parliament.

constituent-assembly.rationale: James holds that the king is author of the laws and that parliament only craves them, so an elected assembly cannot make the fundamental law.

death-penalty.rationale: James says the king has power over the life and death of every subject, and Bossuet cites the ruler's sword as God's to execute wrath on evildoers.

democracy-best.rationale: Bossuet places all the power of individuals and the will of all the people in the person of the prince, so sovereignty belongs to one ruler rather than to the people.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Britannica records that appeal to God added sanction to hereditary right and that the elective principle withered as heredity was established, so the crown is not filled by popular election.

direct-votes.rationale: James holds that laws are made by the king and no parliament can make law without his sceptre, so citizens deciding laws by vote is excluded.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Bossuet states that all power is of God and that the royal throne is the throne of God himself; Britannica describes divine right as the doctrine that kings derived their authority from God.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Britannica records that appeal to God added sanction to hereditary right, and Filmer's divine-right argument has Charles I rule as Adam's eldest heir.

elective-rulers.rationale: Britannica records that appeal to God added sanction to hereditary right and that the elective principle withered as heredity was established, and Filmer's divine-right case makes the king a hereditary father of the realm.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Bodin's sovereignty includes conduct of war and international relations and is absolute, so enforcement by an outside body is excluded.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: James holds the king is above the law and Britannica says absolutism admits no judicial or legislative check, so a charter limiting the ruler is excluded.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: James holds that the king is above the law, which cannot be squared with equal rights before the law for all people.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Bossuet describes the orders going out from the prince's cabinet that make the captains, soldiers and armies on land and sea work in concert.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Bossuet draws politics from the words of Scripture, and Bodin binds even the sovereign to divine law.

leader-cult.rationale: Bossuet calls kings holy things, majesty the image of God in the prince, and says the whole state and the will of all the people are included in him.

minority-veto.rationale: James holds that laws are the king's, made at his pleasure, and Bodin's absolute sovereign's authority is not shared with subjects, so decisions bind without the consent of each.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Bodin says the authority of an absolute sovereign is his own and not shared with any of his subjects, so power is not divided between few and many.

more-religion-public.rationale: Bossuet says there is something religious in the respect due a prince and that the service of God and respect for kings are bound together.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Bossuet says the king needs absolute power to do good as well as repress evil, and James makes the health of the commonwealth his chief law, which is broader than protection from violence.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Bossuet holds that the king's authority is God's and that the only protection of individuals against public authority is their innocence, so subjects owe obedience; Bodin forbids resistance even to a cruel sovereign.

parliament-supreme.rationale: James holds that parliament is only the king's head court and that no law is valid without his sceptre; Bodin calls the idea that the Estates outrank the prince absurd.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Bodin defines sovereignty as the most high, absolute and perpetual power, covering foreign affairs and war as well as internal rule, which cannot be shared with a union.

private-courts-defense.rationale: James makes the king master over every person with power of life and death by laws made by himself, and Britannica says no judicial agency checks the absolutist ruler.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Bodin frees the sovereign from the civil laws he or his predecessors made and James has the king make statutes without parliament, though James adds that a good king will conform to the law.

religion-illusion.rationale: Bossuet and the divine-right doctrine treat God's power and judgment over kings as real, not as illusory comfort.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Bodin holds that against an absolute sovereign no resistance by law or arms is ever permissible, even for cruel and impious deeds, and Bossuet calls any attack on the king sacrilege.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Bodin forbids any attempt on an absolute sovereign by law or force of arms whatever his deeds, and Bossuet treats attacking the king as sacrilege.

right-to-secede.rationale: Bodin defines sovereignty as absolute and perpetual power over the subjects of the commonwealth, which a region's right to leave would end.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Bossuet says the person of the king is sacred and that to attack him in any way is sacrilege.

separate-church-state.rationale: Bossuet says the service of God and respect for kings are bound together, and Britannica notes monarchs asserted authority in both church and state.

separated-powers.rationale: Britannica defines absolutism as ruling power not subject to check by any judicial, legislative, religious, economic or electoral agency, and James holds that no parliament can make law without the king's sceptre.

single-common-good.rationale: James says the health of the commonwealth is the king's chief law and Bossuet says royal power is given for the good of the people.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: James argues that the king is above the law as its author and giver of strength, and Britannica describes the French doctrine as setting the king above the law, subject only to God; Bodin frees the sovereign from civil law while binding him to natural and divine law.

state-harmful.rationale: Bossuet says all the state is in the prince and that, should the king's authority cease in the realm, all would be in confusion.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Bossuet makes the throne God's and binds service of God to respect for kings, which a state teaching atheism would contradict.

strong-leader.rationale: Bossuet holds that without absolute authority the king could neither do good nor repress evil, and Britannica defines absolutism as ruling power not subject to challenge or check by any other agency.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Britannica says the new national monarchs asserted authority in matters of both church and state and tended to become heads of church as well as state, as Henry VIII did.

universal-morality.rationale: Bodin binds every sovereign, including those of France, Spain, Turkey and Persia, to natural and divine law.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Bodin says it is in no circumstances permissible to act against an absolute king even if he has committed all the impious and cruel deeds imaginable.

workers-councils.rationale: James holds that no assembly can make law without the king's sceptre and Britannica defines absolutism as power not checked by any other body, so councils as the basis of political power are excluded.

notes: Enlightened absolutism (see its own profile) would differ on religion, serfdom and reason. Historians such as Mettam doubt the real power of absolutist monarchs, but the profile follows the doctrine.
